units.title: Hard Disk Drives
units.tip: Hard disk drives store data on spinning magnetic platters. A read/write head moves across the platter to access data. They are mechanical, so access time depends on where the data is on the spinning disk.

exercises.question: What is the main component that stores data in a hard disk drive?
exercises.answer: A rotating magnetic platter
exercises.explain: Data is stored as magnetic regions on a thin circular disk coated with magnetic material. As the platter spins, the read/write head accesses data.
choices: A laser beam
A light-emitting crystal
A rotating magnetic platter
A series of transistors

exercises.question: What is a 'read/write head'?
exercises.answer: A tiny electromagnet that reads and writes data on the spinning platter
exercises.explain: The head changes polarity to write data as magnetic bits and detects polarity changes to read. It floats a few nanometers above the platter without touching.
choices: A circuit that controls the spindle
A cooling fan
A tiny electromagnet that reads and writes data on the spinning platter
A spinning motor

exercises.question: What does 'seek time' mean?
exercises.answer: The time for the read/write head to move to the target data location
exercises.explain: Seek time includes the time to physically move the head arm to the correct track. Faster seek times mean quicker data access.
choices: The time for the read/write head to move to the target data location
The time to spin up the platter
The time to power on the drive
The time to write one byte

exercises.question: What is 'rotational latency'?
exercises.answer: The time the platter must spin to bring the desired data under the head
exercises.explain: Once the head reaches the right track, the platter must rotate to present the data under the head. Faster rotation reduces latency.
choices: The time the platter must spin to bring the desired data under the head
The time to read one sector
The delay when the drive first powers on
The cooling time after extended use

exercises.question: Why do hard drive platters keep spinning while the drive is in use?
exercises.answer: To minimize latency and allow fast access to any data location
exercises.explain: Continuous rotation means data is always moving under the head. Stopping and starting between accesses would add large delays.
choices: To prevent data corruption
Because older drives required it
To minimize latency and allow fast access to any data location
To generate heat for the drive to operate

exercises.question: What is a 'sector' on a hard drive?
exercises.answer: The smallest unit of data the drive can read or write
exercises.explain: A sector is a fixed-size block (usually 512 bytes or 4 KB). Data is always read and written in whole sectors.
choices: A section of the platter that has failed
A track that is not used
The smallest unit of data the drive can read or write
A backup copy of data

exercises.question: What is a 'track' on a hard drive?
exercises.answer: A circular path on the platter where data is stored
exercises.explain: The platter is divided into concentric circles (tracks) and radial sections (sectors). Together they form a grid for storing data.
choices: A backup system
A circular path on the platter where data is stored
A defective area of the platter
A cooling channel

exercises.question: What happens if the read/write head crashes into the platter?
exercises.answer: The head and platter can both be damaged, destroying data
exercises.explain: A head crash is catastrophic. The head scratches the platter, damaging both. Data loss is likely and the drive must be replaced.
choices: The drive automatically repairs itself
Nothing; the head is designed to contact the platter
The head and platter can both be damaged, destroying data
Only the head is damaged, data is safe

exercises.question: Why should you not move a hard drive while it is powered on?
exercises.answer: Vibration can cause the head to crash into the platter
exercises.explain: The head floats only nanometers above the platter. Sudden vibration or movement can make it contact the platter, causing data loss.
choices: Because it corrupts the hard drive firmware
Because it wastes power
Vibration can cause the head to crash into the platter
Because it slows down the transfer rate

exercises.question: What is 'S.M.A.R.T. monitoring'?
exercises.answer: Technology that predicts hard drive failures by monitoring key metrics
exercises.explain: S.M.A.R.T. (Self-Monitoring, Analysis and Reporting Technology) tracks things like temperature and error rates. It can often warn before a drive fails, though not always.
choices: A way to repair bad sectors
A method to clean the platter
Technology that predicts hard drive failures by monitoring key metrics
A security feature that encrypts data

units.title: Flash Storage Fundamentals
units.tip: Flash storage uses transistors to store charge, which represents 1s and 0s. Unlike hard drives, flash has no moving parts. However, flash cells wear out with repeated writes.

exercises.question: What is a 'flash memory cell'?
exercises.answer: A transistor that stores electrical charge to represent 1 or 0
exercises.explain: A flash cell traps electrons in a floating gate. The amount of charge determines if it reads as 0 or 1.
choices: A transistor that stores electrical charge to represent 1 or 0
A small area of the platter
A spinning motor
A cooling system

exercises.question: What is the difference between SLC, MLC, and TLC flash?
exercises.answer: They store 1, 2, and 3 bits per cell respectively
exercises.explain: SLC (Single-Level Cell) stores 1 bit, MLC (Multi-Level Cell) stores 2 bits, TLC stores 3 bits. More bits per cell means higher density but shorter lifespan.
choices: They are speed grades for the same technology
They store 1, 2, and 3 bits per cell respectively
Different manufacturers make different types
They are different brands of the same product

exercises.question: What is 'flash memory wear'?
exercises.answer: Degradation of cells after repeated write/erase cycles
exercises.explain: Each write and erase damages the cell's gate insulator. After 1,000 to 100,000 cycles (depending on type), cells fail and cannot hold charge.
choices: The flash becoming slower over time
The physical size of the flash chip decreasing
Dust accumulating on the flash chip
Degradation of cells after repeated write/erase cycles

exercises.question: What is a 'program/erase cycle' (P/E cycle)?
exercises.answer: One complete write and erase of a flash cell
exercises.explain: Each write (program) and erase damages the cell. The number of P/E cycles is the lifespan of the cell.
choices: A data integrity check
A full backup and restore
One complete write and erase of a flash cell
A system reboot

exercises.question: What is 'flash data retention'?
exercises.answer: How long stored charge remains without being refreshed
exercises.explain: Flash cells slowly lose charge over time, especially without power. Retention is important for devices that may be unpowered for long periods.
choices: The cost per byte of storage
How much data can be stored
The speed of reading data
How long stored charge remains without being refreshed

exercises.question: What is 'wear leveling'?
exercises.answer: Distributing writes across all cells to even out wear and extend lifespan
exercises.explain: If the same cells are written repeatedly, they fail first. Wear leveling spreads writes across the entire flash so all cells wear equally.
choices: Distributing writes across all cells to even out wear and extend lifespan
Replacing old cells with new ones
Checking the health of flash cells
A process that smooths the flash surface

exercises.question: What is the 'TRIM command'?
exercises.answer: A signal from the OS telling the drive which blocks are no longer used
exercises.explain: When you delete a file, the OS sends TRIM to tell the drive those blocks are empty. The drive can optimize garbage collection.
choices: A defragmentation process
A tool to reduce file sizes
A signal from the OS telling the drive which blocks are no longer used
A backup command

exercises.question: What is 'garbage collection' in an SSD?
exercises.answer: The process of organizing free blocks and clearing invalid data
exercises.explain: SSDs must consolidate fragmented blocks and erase invalid data to create free space. This happens automatically in the background.
choices: The process of organizing free blocks and clearing invalid data
Deleting corrupt files
Checking disk health
Backing up old data

exercises.question: Why is garbage collection necessary in flash storage?
exercises.answer: Because flash must erase entire blocks even to write to a small part
exercises.explain: Flash organizes data in blocks. To write to one block, the entire block must be erased first. Garbage collection consolidates data to create free blocks.
choices: Because flash must erase entire blocks even to write to a small part
Because the operating system requires it
Because deleted files take up space
Because the drive is damaged

exercises.question: What happens if an SSD runs out of free space for garbage collection?
exercises.answer: Performance degrades because the drive cannot consolidate and erase blocks
exercises.explain: Without free space, the drive cannot move data around efficiently. Writes slow down as the drive struggles to find space.
choices: The drive stops working completely
Performance degrades because the drive cannot consolidate and erase blocks
Files are automatically deleted
Data corruption occurs

units.title: Storage Interfaces
units.tip: Storage devices connect to the computer through interfaces that define the physical connection and protocol. SATA, NVMe, and USB are common interfaces with different speeds and uses.

exercises.question: What does SATA stand for?
exercises.answer: Serial Advanced Technology Attachment
exercises.explain: SATA is a serial interface for connecting hard drives and SSDs. It replaced the older parallel ATA (PATA) interface.
choices: Sequential Array Transfer Architecture
Serial Attachment Technical Architecture
Serial Advanced Technology Attachment
Standard Automatic Transfer Access

exercises.question: What is a key advantage of SATA over older parallel interfaces?
exercises.answer: Simpler cabling and higher speeds despite using fewer wires
exercises.explain: SATA uses fewer pins and thinner cables but achieves faster speeds through better signaling and higher clock rates.
choices: SATA works with more devices
SATA is cheaper to manufacture
Simpler cabling and higher speeds despite using fewer wires
SATA is more secure

exercises.question: What is 'SATA hot-swapping'?
exercises.answer: The ability to connect or disconnect a SATA drive while the computer is powered on
exercises.explain: With a supporting controller and drive bay, SATA drives can be connected or removed without rebooting. This is useful for adding storage or replacing failed drives.
choices: Replacing a SATA cable while in use
Switching between multiple SATA ports
The ability to connect or disconnect a SATA drive while the computer is powered on
Quickly removing and reinstalling the same drive

exercises.question: How many drives does a standard SATA port connect to?
exercises.answer: One drive per port
exercises.explain: SATA is point to point: each port connects to a single drive. A motherboard provides several ports, and the count varies by model.
choices: Up to eight drives
Up to four drives in a daisy chain
One drive per port
As many as the power supply can feed

exercises.question: What is SATA's primary limitation?
exercises.answer: Its maximum speed is lower than faster interfaces like NVMe
exercises.explain: SATA has a bandwidth ceiling. NVMe and other modern interfaces are much faster, so SATA is being phased out for high-performance storage.
choices: It requires constant power
It cannot hot-swap drives
It does not support SSDs
Its maximum speed is lower than faster interfaces like NVMe

exercises.question: What does NVMe stand for?
exercises.answer: Non-Volatile Memory Express
exercises.explain: NVMe is a modern interface designed specifically for flash memory. It is much faster than SATA.
choices: Networked Variable Memory Endpoint
Network Virtual Memory Exchange
New Version Memory Expansion
Non-Volatile Memory Express

exercises.question: What is an advantage of NVMe over SATA?
exercises.answer: Much higher speed and lower latency
exercises.explain: NVMe connects directly to PCIe lanes, bypassing the slower SATA controller. This gives dramatically faster performance.
choices: It is easier to install
Much higher speed and lower latency
It is less expensive
It uses less power

exercises.question: What is an 'M.2' form factor?
exercises.answer: A small, rectangular slot for high-speed storage drives
exercises.explain: M.2 is the physical shape used by most NVMe drives. It plugs directly into an M.2 slot on the motherboard without cables.
choices: A type of hard drive
A USB connector
A small, rectangular slot for high-speed storage drives
A version of SATA

exercises.question: What is the difference between PCIe Gen 3, Gen 4, and Gen 5 NVMe?
exercises.answer: Each generation has double the bandwidth of the previous
exercises.explain: Each PCIe generation roughly doubles the bandwidth per lane of the one before. Generations are backward compatible, so a drive and slot of different generations still work together at the slower one's speed.
choices: They are different brands
There is no practical difference
Each generation has double the bandwidth of the previous
Gen 5 works with all computers; Gen 3 and 4 do not

exercises.question: Can an NVMe drive work through a standard SATA port?
exercises.answer: No, a SATA port uses a different protocol and cannot run NVMe
exercises.explain: NVMe talks over PCIe, while a SATA port speaks the SATA protocol. Some M.2 slots do accept SATA drives, so always check what a slot supports.
choices: Yes, but at reduced speed
No, a SATA port uses a different protocol and cannot run NVMe
Only on some motherboards
Yes, with an adapter

units.title: RAID and Redundancy
units.tip: RAID combines multiple drives to improve performance or reliability. Different RAID levels trade speed, capacity, and redundancy. RAID is not a backup; it protects against drive failure but not data loss.

exercises.question: What does RAID stand for?
exercises.answer: Redundant Array of Independent Disks
exercises.explain: RAID combines multiple drives using software or hardware to improve performance, reliability, or both.
choices: Random Access of Integrated Data
Rapid Array of Integrated Drivers
Recursive Array of Independent Devices
Redundant Array of Independent Disks

exercises.question: What is RAID 0?
exercises.answer: Striping data across multiple drives for speed, with no redundancy
exercises.explain: RAID 0 splits data across drives, so speed scales with the number of drives. But if one drive fails, all data is lost. No redundancy.
choices: Striping data across multiple drives for speed, with no redundancy
Mirroring data for backup
Storing multiple copies of data
Using parity to recover from drive failure

exercises.question: What is RAID 1?
exercises.answer: Mirroring, where identical copies of data exist on two drives
exercises.explain: RAID 1 writes the same data to two drives. If one fails, the other has a complete copy. Good redundancy, but usable capacity is half of the total and writes are no faster.
choices: Combining three or more drives
A faster version of RAID 0
Mirroring, where identical copies of data exist on two drives
Using parity to recover from failure

exercises.question: What is RAID 5?
exercises.answer: Striping with distributed parity to allow recovery from one drive failure
exercises.explain: RAID 5 spreads data and parity across three or more drives. If one fails, the others reconstruct its data. Good balance of speed, capacity, and redundancy.
choices: A combination of RAID 0 and RAID 1
Only for solid-state drives
Five drives in a single array
Striping with distributed parity to allow recovery from one drive failure

exercises.question: What is the capacity overhead of RAID 5?
exercises.answer: One drive's worth of space is used for parity data
exercises.explain: In a 3-drive RAID 5, you get 2 drives' worth of usable space (one drive is parity). In a 4-drive array, you get 3 drives' worth.
choices: Half the space is lost to parity
The overhead depends on the brand of drive
No overhead; all space is usable
One drive's worth of space is used for parity data

exercises.question: What happens when a RAID 5 drive fails?
exercises.answer: The array continues operating with reduced speed while the data is reconstructed
exercises.explain: RAID 5 reconstructs the failed drive's data from parity. Until it finishes, the array runs slower.
choices: The RAID controller automatically replaces the drive
All data is immediately lost
The array continues operating with reduced speed while the data is reconstructed
The array stops completely

exercises.question: How many drives can fail in RAID 5?
exercises.answer: Only one drive can fail without data loss
exercises.explain: RAID 5 protects against one drive failure. If a second drive fails before recovery completes, all data is lost.
choices: Up to half the drives
Unlimited drives can fail
Only one drive can fail without data loss
Two drives can fail

exercises.question: What is the difference between RAID and backup?
exercises.answer: RAID protects against hardware failure; backup protects against data loss
exercises.explain: RAID keeps you running if a drive fails. But if you accidentally delete files or data is corrupted, RAID does not help. Use both.
choices: They are the same thing
RAID is newer than backup
RAID protects against hardware failure; backup protects against data loss
Backup is more expensive

exercises.question: What is RAID reconstruction time?
exercises.answer: The time required to rebuild a failed drive's data from parity
exercises.explain: Reconstruction can take hours or days depending on the array size. During this time, the array is vulnerable to a second failure.
choices: The time to format the array
The time to order a replacement drive
The time between backups
The time required to rebuild a failed drive's data from parity

exercises.question: Why does RAID 5 reconstruction take so long?
exercises.answer: The array must read all remaining drives to reconstruct one drive's worth of data
exercises.explain: Reconstruction is I/O intensive. The array reads every block on every drive to calculate parity and rebuild the failed drive.
choices: Because it encrypts the data
The array must read all remaining drives to reconstruct one drive's worth of data
Because it runs in the background
Because the RAID controller is slow

units.title: File Systems and Data Organization
units.tip: A file system organizes how data is stored on a disk. It manages files, folders, and free space. It also provides features like permissions and journaling to keep data safe.

exercises.question: What does a file system do?
exercises.answer: Organizes data into files and folders and tracks where everything is stored
exercises.explain: A file system is the logical layer on top of raw storage. It divides storage into files, folders, and free space and maintains a directory.
choices: Compresses files to save space
Organizes data into files and folders and tracks where everything is stored
Encrypts data for security
Backs up data automatically

exercises.question: What is an 'inode'?
exercises.answer: A data structure that stores metadata about a file (size, permissions, timestamp)
exercises.explain: An inode tracks file information like size, owner, permissions, and the location of data blocks. The file name is separate from the inode.
choices: A type of encryption
A data structure that stores metadata about a file (size, permissions, timestamp)
A block of data
A hard link

exercises.question: What is 'fragmentation'?
exercises.answer: When a file is split across non-contiguous blocks on disk
exercises.explain: Fragmentation happens when files are written, deleted, and rewritten over time. Fragments slow down access because the head must move more.
choices: The number of files on a disk
When a file is split across non-contiguous blocks on disk
A disk is broken into pieces
A type of data corruption

exercises.question: Why is fragmentation less of a problem with SSDs than with hard drives?
exercises.answer: SSDs have no moving head, so access time is the same regardless of location
exercises.explain: Hard drives must seek to different parts of the platter, so fragmentation slows them down. SSDs access all locations equally fast.
choices: SSDs do not use fragmentation
SSDs have no moving head, so access time is the same regardless of location
SSDs automatically defragment
TRIM prevents all fragmentation

exercises.question: What is 'journaling' in a file system?
exercises.answer: Logging changes to a journal before writing to disk to prevent corruption
exercises.explain: Journaling records what the file system is about to change. If the system crashes, the journal helps recover without corruption.
choices: Logging changes to a journal before writing to disk to prevent corruption
Tracking file history
Keeping records of file access
Backing up files regularly

exercises.question: What is a backup?
exercises.answer: A copy of data stored separately from the original
exercises.explain: Backups protect against accidental deletion, corruption, and hardware failure. They are not the same as RAID.
choices: A system that prevents deletions
A second copy on the same drive
A copy of data stored separately from the original
Part of the file system

exercises.question: What is the '3-2-1 backup rule'?
exercises.answer: Keep 3 copies of data: 2 on different media, 1 offsite
exercises.explain: 3 copies protect against multiple failure modes. 2 different media types protect against format-specific problems. Offsite protects against disaster.
choices: Keep 3 copies in the same location
Backup 3 times per day, 2 days a week, 1 time per month
Backup to 3 different companies
Keep 3 copies of data: 2 on different media, 1 offsite

exercises.question: What is an 'incremental backup'?
exercises.answer: Backing up only the files that changed since the last backup
exercises.explain: Incremental backups are fast and save space because they only back up new or modified files.
choices: Backing up in increasing order of size
Backing up one file at a time
Backing up only the files that changed since the last backup
A full backup every time

exercises.question: What is a 'full backup'?
exercises.answer: Backing up all data regardless of when it was last backed up
exercises.explain: A full backup takes more time and space but is complete and easy to restore. Incremental backups are faster but require all previous increments.
choices: Backing up every file only once
A backup that never needs to be done again
Backing up all data regardless of when it was last backed up
A backup that fills the drive completely

exercises.question: Why should backups be stored offsite?
exercises.answer: To protect against disasters like fire or theft that destroy local data
exercises.explain: If your home or office burns down, a backup in the same building is worthless. Offsite backups protect against physical disasters.
choices: To protect against disasters like fire or theft that destroy local data
Because it is faster
Because offsite storage is more secure
Because it is cheaper

units.title: Other Storage Technologies
units.tip: Beyond hard drives and SSDs, optical media (CDs, DVDs) and tape storage serve specific purposes. Each has different characteristics for cost, speed, lifespan, and use cases.

exercises.question: How does a CD store data?
exercises.answer: As pits and lands (bumps and flat areas) in a reflective layer
exercises.explain: A laser reads the pits and lands. Pits scatter light; lands reflect it. The pattern represents 1s and 0s.
choices: As color patterns on the disk
Using magnetic charges
As pits and lands (bumps and flat areas) in a reflective layer
As electrical charges in transistors

exercises.question: What is the difference between a CD, DVD, and Blu-ray?
exercises.answer: They use increasingly smaller pits and shorter laser wavelengths to store more data
exercises.explain: CDs use a 780nm laser, DVDs use 650nm, and Blu-rays use 405nm. Shorter wavelengths read smaller pits, so Blu-rays hold more data in the same physical size.
choices: DVDs and Blu-rays require special players
They are made from different materials
Only one type is rewritable
They use increasingly smaller pits and shorter laser wavelengths to store more data

exercises.question: What is 'disc rot' in optical media?
exercises.answer: Degradation of the reflective layer over time, causing data errors
exercises.explain: The dyes and coatings in optical disks fade over years or decades. Eventually, pits become unreadable.
choices: Scratches on the disk surface
The disk spinning too fast
Dust accumulating on the disk
Degradation of the reflective layer over time, causing data errors

exercises.question: What is the lifespan of a CD, DVD, or Blu-ray disk?
exercises.answer: Highly variable, from a few years to many decades depending on manufacturing quality and storage conditions
exercises.explain: Good quality disks in cool, dry storage may last decades. Poor quality or hot storage may fail in a few years. Test old disks.
choices: Always exactly 10 years
Indefinite if kept in any environment
Highly variable, from a few years to many decades depending on manufacturing quality and storage conditions
Less than 1 year always

exercises.question: What does the 'R' in CD-R mean?
exercises.answer: Recordable: it can be written once
exercises.explain: A CD-R has a dye layer that a laser burns once. CD-RW discs can be erased and rewritten, and CD-ROM discs are pressed at the factory and are read-only.
choices: Recordable: it can be written once
Rapid: it spins faster
Read-only: it cannot be written at all
Rewritable: it can be erased and rewritten many times

exercises.question: What is magnetic tape used for?
exercises.answer: Long-term archival and backup of large data sets
exercises.explain: Tape is cheap per gigabyte for storage over decades. It is sequential, not random-access, so it is slow for day-to-day use.
choices: Portable storage devices
Long-term archival and backup of large data sets
Fast database access
Real-time streaming

exercises.question: What is an advantage of tape over hard drives for archival?
exercises.answer: Much lower cost per gigabyte and longer data retention
exercises.explain: Tape is very cheap per gigabyte for large data volumes and can store data for decades in the right conditions.
choices: Easier to use
Much lower cost per gigabyte and longer data retention
More durable physically
Faster access speed

exercises.question: What is 'sequential access' in tape storage?
exercises.answer: Data must be read in order from the beginning, not randomly
exercises.explain: Tape is like a cassette: you must fast-forward to the data you want. Hard drives and SSDs allow random access to any location instantly.
choices: Data can only be accessed once
Data is accessed in alphabetical order
Multiple people cannot access it at the same time
Data must be read in order from the beginning, not randomly

exercises.question: Why is tape slow for random access?
exercises.answer: The tape must physically move to the desired location, taking seconds to minutes
exercises.explain: There is no 'jump to' operation. The tape drive must spool through the tape mechanically.
choices: The tape must physically move to the desired location, taking seconds to minutes
Because it uses magnetic storage
Because it is old technology
Because tape is made of plastic

exercises.question: What is the typical use case for LTO (Linear Tape-Open) tapes?
exercises.answer: Enterprise-grade long-term backup and archival
exercises.explain: LTO is the standard for data centers and institutions that need to preserve terabytes of data for years.
choices: Real-time database access
Streaming video
Personal computer backup
Enterprise-grade long-term backup and archival
